newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat says U.S. against "Judaizing" Jerusalem.
newsitem.headline: Arafat says U.S. against "Judaizing" Jerusalem.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said on his return to Gaza on Saturday that the United States was against the "Judaization" of Jerusalem.

Asked by reporters if U.S. peace envoy Dennis Ross had asked him to calm tensions in Palestinian Authority areas abutting Israeli army positions where there have been clashes since Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement, Arafat replied:
"Yes, they are against the violence, especially the violence of settlement and the Judaization of Jerusalem."

Peace moves between the Palestinians and Israel plunged into crisis this month after Israel broke ground on a new Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem and an Islamist suicide bombing in Tel Aviv that killed three Israelis.

Israel says Arafat gave militants the impression they had a green light to carry out attacks. The Authority denies the charge. Palestinians see building in Jerusalem as preempting negotiations that are to be held on its status in final peace talks which have yet to resume.
U.S. envoy Dennis Ross wound up a two-day emergency shuttle on Friday appealing for calm after finding Israelis and Palestinians in no mood for compromise.
He had met Arafat in Rabat and then Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. The White House called the mission "constructive" but said more work was needed.
Netanyahu said after meeting Ross that only a sustained Palestinian crackdown on "terrorism" -- not just a pledge to fight militants -- would salvage peacemaking.
Arafat told reporters in Gaza: "Netanyahu's orders and decisions are escalating the situation in the whole area."
The Authority insists the only way out of the crisis is for Israel to order its bulldozers to stop ripping up an Arab East Jerusalem hillside to build the new Jewish settlement.
Arafat was to convene his cabinet in Gaza on Saturday night. He has been away for seven days on an Asian and African tour.

He returns as thousands of Israeli police, backed by tanks and helicopters in the West Bank, remained on high alert ahead of warnings of potential clashes on Sunday -- the annual "Land Day" when Israeli Arabs stage protests against government land confiscations.
